title: Inverted index construction
description: An inverted index maps every term to the list of documents containing it, turning full-text search into fast dictionary lookups. Tokenize each document, then for every term append the document ID to that term's posting list in a hash map; sorting or hashing terms gives O(1) term lookup and the postings enable boolean and ranked queries. It is the foundational structure behind nearly all text search. Use it as the core of any archive search engine.
provenance: public-harvest: established computer-science methods documented in standard literature and practice

t: B+ tree for ordered archive keys
title: B+ tree for ordered archive keys
description: A B+ tree keeps archive keys sorted across balanced pages so range scans and ordered lookups stay fast as data grows. Keys live in leaf pages linked in order, with internal pages holding separator keys; every leaf sits at the same depth, so lookups cost O(log n) page reads and range scans just walk the leaf chain. High fan-out keeps the tree shallow even for millions of keys. Use it for ID-ordered archive indexes and sorted range queries.
demo:
import bisect
leaves = [[1, 4, 9], [12, 18, 25], [30, 44]]
def bplus_find(key):
    for leaf in leaves:
        i = bisect.bisect_left(leaf, key)
        if i < len(leaf) and leaf[i] == key: return leaf
    return None
print("key 18 ->", bplus_find(18))
assert bplus_find(18) == [12, 18, 25]
assert bplus_find(99) is None
provenance: public-harvest: established computer-science methods documented in standard literature and practice

t: Log-structured merge tree for write-heavy indexing
title: Log-structured merge tree for write-heavy indexing
description: An LSM tree absorbs index writes in memory and merges them into sorted disk levels, trading read amplification for very fast writes. New postings go to an in-memory memtable; when full it flushes as an immutable sorted run, and background compactions merge runs level by level. Bloom filters on each run skip most disk reads, keeping point lookups practical. Use it when the archive ingests documents far faster than it serves queries.
provenance: public-harvest: established computer-science methods documented in standard literature and practice

t: Delta-encoded posting lists with variable integers
title: Delta-encoded posting lists with variable integers
description: Delta encoding stores sorted document IDs as gaps between consecutive IDs, shrinking posting lists dramatically since gaps are small numbers. Each gap is written as a variable-length integer (7 bits per byte with a continuation bit), so small gaps cost one byte; decoding reconstructs IDs by cumulative sum. This is the standard compression for inverted index postings. Use it to fit large archive posting lists in memory or cut index size on disk.
provenance: public-harvest: established computer-science methods documented in standard literature and practice

title: Skip lists inside posting lists
description: Skip pointers let posting-list intersection jump over blocks of document IDs instead of scanning every entry. Every k-th posting stores a forward pointer to the posting k steps ahead; intersecting two lists advances the lagging pointer by skips until it catches up, then scans finely. This cuts AND-query cost from linear toward sublinear in list length. Use it to speed up multi-term archive queries over long posting lists.
demo:
def with_skips(postings, k=3):
    return [(doc, postings[i+k] if i+k < len(postings) else None)
            for i, doc in enumerate(postings) if i % k == 0]
a = list(range(0, 100, 2)); b = list(range(0, 100, 3))
inter, i, j = [], 0, 0
while i < len(a) and j < len(b):
    if a[i] == b[j]: inter.append(a[i]); i += 1; j += 1
    elif a[i] < b[j]: i += 1
    else: j += 1
print("intersection size:", len(inter), "skip table entries:", len(with_skips(a)))
assert inter == list(range(0, 100, 6))
provenance: public-harvest: established computer-science methods documented in standard literature and practice

t: Bitmap indexes for low-cardinality archive fields
title: Bitmap indexes for low-cardinality archive fields
description: A bitmap index represents each distinct field value as a bit vector over documents, so filtering becomes fast bitwise AND/OR operations. One bit per document per value; a query like category=news AND year=2024 is a single AND of two bit arrays, often accelerated with run-length compression (WAH/Roaring). They excel when fields have few distinct values across many documents. Use it for faceted archive filtering over categories, years, and flags.
demo:
docs = ["news", "blog", "news", "wiki", "blog", "news"]
bitmaps = {}
for i, v in enumerate(docs):
    bm = bitmaps.setdefault(v, [0]*len(docs)); bm[i] = 1
news = bitmaps["news"]
print("news bitmap:", news)
hits = [i for i, b in enumerate(news) if b]
print("matching docs:", hits)
assert hits == [0, 2, 5]
provenance: public-harvest: established computer-science methods documented in standard literature and practice

t: Index segment merging for live archives
title: Index segment merging for live archives
description: Segment merging folds small fresh index segments into larger ones so the archive stays queryable while new documents stream in. New documents build a small in-memory segment; a merge policy (e.g., tiered: merge N same-size segments) k-way merges their sorted postings into a bigger segment, deleting merged-away tombstones. Queries fan out across the few live segments and merge results. Use it to keep an archive searchable during continuous ingestion.
demo:
import heapq
segs = [[1, 4, 9], [2, 5], [3, 6, 8]]
merged = list(heapq.merge(*segs))
print("segments:", segs)
print("merged:", merged)
assert merged == sorted([1, 4, 9, 2, 5, 3, 6, 8])
provenance: public-harvest: established computer-science methods documented in standard literature and practice

title: Live document updates with tombstones
description: Tombstones mark deleted or replaced documents in the index without rewriting posting lists, deferring the real cleanup to merge time. An update writes the new version's postings plus a tombstone record for the old document ID; queries filter out tombstoned IDs, and segment merges physically drop them. This makes updates O(1)-ish instead of requiring posting-list surgery. Use it for archives where documents are corrected or withdrawn over time.
provenance: public-harvest: established computer-science methods documented in standard literature and practice

t: Forward index for reindexing and highlighting
title: Forward index for reindexing and highlighting
description: A forward index maps each document to its terms, enabling reindexing, snippet highlighting, and 'more like this' without re-parsing source text. While building the inverted index the indexer also stores per-document term vectors; rebuilding a term's postings or highlighting query hits then reads the forward index directly. It doubles as the store for document metadata and term statistics. Use it to support result snippets and index rebuilds in the archive.
provenance: public-harvest: established computer-science methods documented in standard literature and practice

title: TF-IDF term scoring
description: TF-IDF scores a document by how often a query term appears in it, discounted by how common the term is across the whole archive. Term frequency is normalized by document length; inverse document frequency is log(N / df), so rare discriminating terms outweigh ubiquitous ones. The product ranks documents by topical relevance for the query. Use it as the baseline relevance ranker for archive search.
demo:
import math
docs = [["fox", "fox", "dog"], ["fox"], ["dog", "dog", "dog"]]
N = len(docs)
def tfidf(term, doc):
    tf = doc.count(term) / len(doc)
    df = sum(1 for d in docs if term in d)
    return tf * math.log(N / df)
print("tfidf(fox, doc0) =", round(tfidf("fox", docs[0]), 3))
print("tfidf(dog, doc2) =", round(tfidf("dog", docs[2]), 3))
assert tfidf("fox", docs[0]) > tfidf("dog", docs[0])
provenance: public-harvest: established computer-science methods documented in standard literature and practice

title: BM25 ranked retrieval
description: BM25 refines TF-IDF with term-frequency saturation and document-length normalization, and remains the standard baseline for ranked text retrieval. The score sums over query terms: IDF * (tf*(k1+1)) / (tf + k1*(1-b+b*len/avglen)); k1 caps the benefit of repeated terms and b penalizes long documents. With k1=1.2 and b=0.75 it beats plain TF-IDF on most benchmarks. Use it as the default ranking function for the archive's search.
demo:
import math
docs = [["fox"]*5 + ["dog"], ["fox"], ["dog"]*4]
N, avglen = len(docs), sum(map(len, docs))/len(docs)
k1, b = 1.2, 0.75
def bm25(term, doc):
    tf = doc.count(term)
    df = sum(1 for d in docs if term in d)
    idf = math.log(1 + (N - df + 0.5)/(df + 0.5))
    return idf * (tf*(k1+1)) / (tf + k1*(1-b+b*len(doc)/avglen))
scores = [bm25("fox", d) for d in docs]
print("BM25 scores:", [round(s, 3) for s in scores])
assert scores[0] > scores[1] > scores[2]
provenance: public-harvest: established computer-science methods documented in standard literature and practice

t: Field-weighted scoring across title and body
title: Field-weighted scoring across title and body
description: Field-weighted scoring boosts term matches in important fields like titles over matches buried in body text. Each field gets a weight (title 3x, headings 2x, body 1x); the document score sums per-field term scores times their weights. This simple change usually beats uniform scoring because titles concentrate a document's aboutness. Use it when archive records have structured fields of differing importance.
provenance: public-harvest: established computer-science methods documented in standard literature and practice

t: Bloom filter pre-check before posting lookup
title: Bloom filter pre-check before posting lookup
description: A Bloom filter is a compact bit array that answers 'definitely not present / possibly present' for terms, skipping expensive posting lookups for absent terms. k hash functions set k bits per inserted term; a query term hashing to any zero bit is certainly absent. With m bits and n terms the false-positive rate is about (1 - e^(-kn/m))^k, tunable by sizing. Use it in front of the posting index to reject no-hit query terms cheaply.
demo:
import hashlib
m, k = 64, 3
bits = [0]*m
def hashes(t): return [int(hashlib.md5(f"{t}{i}".encode()).hexdigest(), 16) % m for i in range(k)]
for t in ["fox", "dog", "archive"]: 
    for h in hashes(t): bits[h] = 1
def maybe(t): return all(bits[h] for h in hashes(t))
print("maybe('fox'):", maybe("fox"), "| maybe('zebra'):", maybe("zebra"))
assert maybe("fox") and not maybe("zebra")
provenance: public-harvest: established computer-science methods documented in standard literature and practice

t: Trie for prefix and autocomplete lookup
title: Trie for prefix and autocomplete lookup
description: A trie stores the archive's vocabulary as a character tree so prefix searches and autocompletion walk down shared prefixes in O(p) time. Each node holds child edges per character and a terminal flag; inserting a term walks or creates nodes, and prefix lookup collects all terminals in the subtree. It shares storage across terms with common prefixes. Use it for archive search-as-you-type and prefix queries.
provenance: public-harvest: established computer-science methods documented in standard literature and practice

title: Suffix array for substring search
description: A suffix array sorts all suffixes of the archive text, turning substring search into a binary search over the sorted suffixes. Build the array of suffix start positions sorted lexicographically; a query binary-searches for the range of suffixes starting with the pattern, each hit mapping back to a document offset. It finds any substring without tokenization. Use it for exact-phrase and substring search over raw archive text.
demo:
text = "the archive holds archived articles$"
suffixes = sorted(range(len(text)), key=lambda i: text[i:])
def find(pat):
    lo = [i for i in suffixes if text[i:].startswith(pat)]
    return lo
hits = find("archiv")
print("substring 'archiv' at offsets:", hits)
assert len(hits) == 2
provenance: public-harvest: established computer-science methods documented in standard literature and practice
